Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
The world is a dangerous place
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'permanently humiliated' is hard to reconcile unless the illness involved a specifically shaming interpersonal circumstance; nothing else in the profile suggests that context. The other items center danger, fear, vivid reliving, and generalized threat, so humiliation stands out as clinically mismatched to the trauma type.

vignette:
Thomas Avery was seventy-eight when he was hospitalized with a sudden, life-threatening illness that began at home and ended in the intensive care unit. He had been a meticulous database administrator for years, still working part-time from a home office after most men his age had retired, and he was used to trusting systems that behaved predictably. The illness shattered that assumption. He remembered the speed with which his body failed him: the shortness of breath, the confusion, the humiliating dependence on strangers moving quickly around his bed while machines alarmed and oxygen hissed beside him. What remained with him most powerfully was not a coherent story but sensory fragments. Even months later, when the memory came, he could smell the sharp antiseptic and the plastic, medical odor of tubing and oxygen. In those moments he did not feel as if he were recalling something from the past; he felt as though he were back in that hospital bed, with the scene more vivid and immediate than ordinary memory, as if it were happening again in the present.

After he was discharged, Thomas expected gratitude and relief. Instead he found himself unsettled by how little safety meant to him now. He could be sitting in his own living room and still feel on guard, listening to his breathing, noticing every flutter in his chest, every shift in his stomach. At home, where he had once felt most at ease, he began scanning for signs that something catastrophic was about to happen again. The watchfulness had a grim logic for him. He had learned, as he saw it, that danger could come from inside his own body without warning. He was left with strong waves of fear and anger, and under them a hard bitterness that life itself had become unreliable.

The quality of his memories seemed to deepen these conclusions. When the smell of disinfectant or even a chemically clean scent drifted up while he was wiping down his desk or opening supplies in his home office, he could be pulled straight back into the worst moments of the illness. In those episodes, the memory felt more real than the room he was standing in. What frightened him most was what he took these experiences to mean. He had come to believe that his body was no longer his ally, that it kept reacting as if he were still in mortal danger because, in some essential way, the danger had never really passed. The vivid reliving did not feel like memory to him; it felt like proof. From there, his thinking darkened further. If his own body could turn on him so suddenly, then the world was not orderly or benevolent but fundamentally dangerous, and whatever faith he had once had in life's fairness had eroded.

His constant state of alertness reinforced the same beliefs. Thomas found himself checking locks, checking his pulse, checking whether he could take a full breath, even when he knew rationally he was home and medically stable. He was superalert to noises in the apartment at night and equally watchful of sensations inside himself during the day. The more he lived in this keyed-up state, the more convinced he became that his system was warning him of something real. He was certain that if he let his guard down, he would miss the next sign and pay for it. That vigilance fed his sense that the world was dangerous and his body an enemy that might betray him again at any moment. The emotional toll was immediate: fear first, then anger, and sometimes a bleak, almost ashamed sense of how completely his confidence had collapsed.

These changes began to shape his daily life. Because he still managed databases remotely, his work should have offered routine, but even there he was not free of reminders. The sterile smell of packaged electronics, cleaning wipes on his keyboard, and the enclosed quiet of long hours at his desk could all sharpen his awareness of his body and leave him braced for disaster rather than absorbed in the task. He remained functional, but with increasing effort, and his world narrowed around the project of staying ready. As a divorced man living alone, there was no one present to interrupt the private logic that had taken hold.

By the time he sought help, Thomas was exhausted by living as though survival still depended on unbroken vigilance. He spoke less about the illness itself than about what it had done to his view of existence. He no longer trusted life, no longer trusted his body, and no longer felt truly safe even in his own home. What finally brought him in was the recognition that the memories were not fading and that his days were being organized around threat rather than work, rest, or pleasure. He said he wanted, more than anything, to feel that being alive did not have to mean being on guard every minute, but he was afraid that lowering his guard would be the moment something terrible happened again.
